vignette:
Ben still measures the world in frames, but the frames have gotten smaller. Before, his frame was the entire world. As a photojournalist, he chased light across continents, from the sun-bleached plains of Africa to the neon-soaked alleys of Tokyo. The click of the shutter was his native tongue, a language he used to tell stories of conflict, humanity, and fleeting beauty. He was confident, quick on his feet, and possessed an uncanny ability to find the single, perfect image that held the truth of a moment. His wife, Sarah, used to say he had an extra sense, an eye that saw the world not just as it was, but as a story waiting to be told.

That all changed twelve years ago on an assignment in a war-torn border region. It wasn't a firefight or an explosion that broke him, but the sudden, jarring silence. One moment he was framing a shot of a child's worn-out sandal in the dust, and the next, a rough burlap sack was thrown over his head. The world dissolved into the smell of stale sweat, dirt, and fear.

For the next forty-three days, his world was a ten-by-ten-foot concrete cell. They took his cameras, his watch, his boots. They took the light. His captors were ghosts, their faces unseen, their voices muffled and indistinct. The only sensory details he could cling to were the damp chill of the floor, the metallic taste of the water, and the maddeningly irregular rhythm of footsteps in the corridor outside. He lost track of time, marking days by the thin slice of watery soup and stale bread pushed through a slot in the door. His photographer's eye, starved of light and color, turned inward, replaying every mistake, every risk he'd ever taken, over and over. He wasn't a storyteller anymore; he was a trapped animal.

His release was as abrupt and confusing as his capture. One night, he was dragged out, driven for hours, and pushed onto a dusty road, blinking in the blinding moonlight. When he finally made it home, Sarah held him so tightly he felt his ribs might crack, but he felt nothing. He was a hollowed-out version of the man who had left.

In the years since, Ben has tried to reclaim his life, but the cell is always there, waiting at the edges of his perception. He can no longer take international assignments. The thought of a long flight, of being contained in a metal tube, is unbearable. He tries to focus on local work-weddings, corporate headshots, landscapes-but the camera feels alien in his hands. Looking through the viewfinder feels like looking through the slot in his cell door, a narrow, confining view of a world he no longer trusts.

His symptoms manifest in quiet, insidious ways. He can't sleep in a fully dark room and insists on leaving the closet door wide open. A car backfiring on their quiet suburban street sends him diving to the floor before he can even process the sound. He meticulously plans his trips to the grocery store for off-peak hours, unable to handle the press of a crowd, the feeling of being surrounded. He finds himself constantly scanning faces, assessing threats, mapping exit routes in cafes and movie theaters.

Sarah says living with him is like living with a ghost who is terrified of other ghosts. He's physically present, but his mind is elsewhere, patrolling the perimeter of his long-gone prison. He'll be watching television with her, and she'll see his eyes go distant and glassy. She knows he's no longer in their living room; he's back on the cold concrete floor, listening for footsteps. He feels a profound, unbridgeable distance from her, from everyone. He sees their love and concern, but it feels like a photograph of an emotion, a two-dimensional representation of something he can no longer truly feel. He looks at his old, award-winning photographs, images of profound human connection and resilience, and feels nothing but the cold certainty that the man who took them is gone forever.
